comparator.name: Religious Studies
comparator.sourceNotes: The Dutch-taught full-time bachelor comprises 60 EC per year, including some English-taught courses. The adopted 2026–2027 programme regulation lists Arabic first among the permitted first-year subject packages; the dated guide specifies its four 6 EC language courses. This neutral illustration retains the common Religious Studies curriculum, 30 EC of open choice and an 18 EC thesis trajectory. It excludes the shortened programme and other first-year packages. The degree has no formal graduation tracks.
components: The first year also requires a Dutch writing diagnostic. Tutoring and study guidance continue throughout the degree. These requirements carry no credits.

This example uses the 24 EC first-year Arabic package. Students choose one package in another discipline; this does not create a separate graduation track.

Attend Arabic 3 before starting Arabic 4. The sequence develops Egyptian Arabic and then Modern Standard Arabic.

Post-first-year courses require a positive binding study recommendation. The ordinary full-time threshold is 48 first-year EC. Complete Secrets of the West 1 before 2, and both before the research project.
Secrets of the West 2: Culture and Counterculture in the Modern Period
Secrets of the West 3: Culture and Counterculture Research Project
Religion and Spirituality in the Netherlands 1: Concepts and Theories
Religion and Spirituality in the Netherlands 2: Lived Religion
Complete Concepts and Theories before Lived Religion, and both before the Netherlands research project. Students use qualitative methods to investigate contemporary religious practice.
Religion, Art and Culture 2: Sacred Stories in Words and Images
Religion and Spirituality in the Netherlands 3: Research Project
Utopias and Visions of the Future
Bachelor’s Thesis Research Project in Religious Studies

Complete the first year and all compulsory second-year courses before starting. Register for the thesis at the same time. A supervisor must approve the research plan before the first thesis section is written.

Use this 30 EC for electives, a minor, an approved exchange or a placement. Normally no more than 12 EC may be introductory; an approved UvA minor or a same-language sequence can permit up to 24 EC. External study requires Examination Board approval. A placement may occupy up to 12 EC; the Religious Studies and Western Esotericism minors cannot duplicate the compulsory curriculum.
The 12 EC thesis follows the 6 EC research project. Complete the first year and compulsory second-year courses, and pass the research project before the thesis can be assessed.

exception.reason: UCR offers substantial related study in comparative myth, religious art and material culture, ancient ritual, philosophy, social inquiry and religious freedom. These connections do not develop into sustained study of religious traditions, sacred interpretation or contemporary religious practice across a full programme. The wider course combinations shift towards general cultural, philosophical or social study.

exception.ucrCourseEvidence: Three complete 24-course trials were tested against current course content and passed current offering and prerequisite checks. The strongest combines myth, literature, religious visual and material culture, philosophy and qualitative inquiry. Social-public and spirituality-cultural trials test the remaining generator interests. Relevant taught religion, myth, ritual and Buddhist thought receive full weight; general methods and adjacent topics do not establish the missing sustained religious inquiry. The conclusion does not depend on Arabic training, a degree title, a professional licence, missing planning coverage or the number of one-to-one course matches.

candidateAssessment.concept: Comparative religious meaning through texts, images and material culture
candidateAssessment.assessment: The closest trial combines comparative myth, literary reading, art, archaeology, religion and ritual in ancient democracy, philosophy and qualitative inquiry. Myth and religious visual or material meaning are substantive bridges. Additional literary, art-historical and social methods broaden the composition, but their documented teaching does not sustain the target’s investigation of religious traditions, sacred interpretation and lived religious practice. This is a coherent humanities composition whose object becomes wider cultural meaning, rather than a defensible whole-programme response to Religious Studies.

candidateAssessment.concept: Religion in society, identity, public life and conflict
candidateAssessment.assessment: The second trial tests social theory and qualitative research with rights, political authority, comparative institutions, conflict, social psychology and extremism prevention. Freedom of religion, religious constitutions and religion in reconciliation are real taught connections, and documentary and Indigenous history supply further forms of situated inquiry. The general courses do not document a continuing investigation of religious institutions, secularisation, religious pluralism or religious communities. Selecting a religious project topic cannot supply taught subject matter or supervision that the evidence does not establish.

candidateAssessment.concept: Lived religion, spirituality and cultural change
candidateAssessment.assessment: The third trial tests philosophical selfhood, ethics and emotion together with myth, life narrative, art, media and documentary. Buddhist non-self, spiritual self-fashioning, religious visual meaning and ancient ritual are specific relevant contributions. The wider philosophy and media sequence studies general agency, representation and culture; it does not establish sustained contemporary spirituality, Western esotericism or the empirical study of lived religion. General coherence does not repair that target-level shortfall.

audience.programmeDescription: Religious Studies at the University of Amsterdam studies religious diversity, traditions, texts and practices through historical, literary and social-scientific approaches. The programme gives particular attention to contemporary religion and spirituality, Western esotericism and research in Amsterdam. This example includes the first-year Arabic package.
